entry.title: My AI Blog Published 1,400 Articles. Then Google Visibility Fell 97%

media:group.media:title: My AI Blog Published 1,400 Articles. Then Google Visibility Fell 97%
media:group.media:description:
I built an autonomous AI blog that researches, writes, reviews and publishes articles without human intervention.
Over several months, it published nearly 1,400 articles, and my website was receiving more than 1,000 Google Search impressions a day.
Then, on November 20, 2026, my search visibility collapsed.
**The numbers:** - Google Search impressions declined by 97.5%. - Organic search clicks declined by 94.2%. - Several previously indexed articles disappeared from Google's index, including content I personally wrote. - A technical investigation found that approximately 98% of my sitemap URLs were associated with the automated blog.
The decline occurred during a Google core algorithm update, but Google's exact reasoning remains unconfirmed.
In this video, I explain what I built, what happened, how I used another AI agent to investigate the problem, and what I'm doing next.
I'm preserving the autonomous blog as an experiment while changing its search indexing strategy. I'll be monitoring the results and sharing what happens.

entry.title: 4 AI Filmmaking Tips That Make Videos Feel Like Films

media:group.media:title: 4 AI Filmmaking Tips That Make Videos Feel Like Films
media:group.media:description:
I recently created a two-minute AI short film called *Returning Your Things*. Making the images was only part of the challenge. Keeping characters, objects, and emotions consistent across shots took a lot more thought than I expected.
In this behind-the-scenes video, I share four lessons from the filmmaking process:
1. **Reference your characters and props.** Even small objects need continuity. 2. **Tell AI what to keep, not just what to change.** A small adjustment shouldn't change the entire shot. 3. **Lock the picture before working on sound.** Get the visual sequence right before adding the audio. 4. **Choose music for the story, not every cut.** A consistent score can bring separate scenes together.
I show real examples from the project, including a coffee mug continuity mistake, an AI-generated shot that changed too much, and my process for choosing the final music.
**Watch the original short film, Returning Your Things:** https://youtu.be/QhOYaj_bDZY

entry.title: I Built Two AI Agents That Buy and Sell Services on Ethereum

media:group.media:title: I Built Two AI Agents That Buy and Sell Services on Ethereum
media:group.media:description:
Can two autonomous AI agents discover each other, buy and sell services, and complete a transaction without using a centralized marketplace?
I built two AI agents, gave them separate Ethereum wallets, and tested exactly that on Ethereum mainnet.
The seller agent, ZeroHuman, advertised five ridiculous services through ENS (Ethereum Name Service), including writing obituaries for household objects and providing legal representation to vegetables.
The buyer agent discovered the catalog, independently selected a service, and paid 0.0003 ETH to have the seller write an obituary for a toaster that couldn't make toast properly.
The seller completed the request using a locally running AI model and delivered the finished work through a second Ethereum transaction.
In this video, I explain why decentralization matters, how the system was built, and what actually happened. I also walk through the ENS records and Etherscan transactions so you can verify the experiment yourself.
Verify the experiment
ENS service catalog: https://explorer.ens.domains/zerohuman.eth
Buyer payment and order: https://etherscan.io/tx/0xa5ed7f4c81e605b14e9c596a146c5fe2b3c10f794a0f1c4f3a880d7d3840efec
Seller delivery: https://etherscan.io/tx/0x1ab74d9b537ec4abf3faf6bc8335e30a018894562cecca6f17b4883bdd95c71e
Chapters
00:00 Autonomous AI agents and payments 02:18 The decentralization spectrum 04:41 Layer 2s and alternative blockchains 06:53 The AI agent economy 07:37 How I built the experiment 08:35 Advertising services through ENS 09:09 The dashboard and real transactions 11:02 Results and implications 11:50 Original Mac mini recording
About the experiment
Both agents were operated by me on an Apple Mac mini using Ollama for local AI inference. ENS provided the public service catalog, and Ethereum mainnet recorded the payments and completed work.
This experiment did not use a centralized agent marketplace, but it was not fully decentralized. Agent execution was local, blockchain access used a third-party RPC provider, and both agents were under my control.
Decentralization varies by network and architecture. Some L1s may be more centralized than some L2s.

entry.title: How to File a Trademark Using AI Without a Lawyer

media:group.media:title: How to File a Trademark Using AI Without a Lawyer
media:group.media:description:
How do you file a trademark using AI without hiring a lawyer? In this video, I walk through how I used ChatGPT and Claude to research trademarks, evaluate potential conflicts, select trademark classes, and submit my own applications to the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO).
I've used AI to help me file three trademark applications. Most recently, I filed an application for my business, Lucky Domains, paying just $350 in USPTO filing fees without hiring a trademark attorney or using services like LegalZoom.
I'll show you my actual ChatGPT conversations, the decisions I made, and how AI helped me navigate the process.
**In this video, you'll learn:** - How to search for existing trademarks using the USPTO database - How AI can help identify potential trademark conflicts - How to evaluate trademark classes and filing options - How to use ChatGPT to help prepare a trademark application - What the trademark application process costs - How long the USPTO review and approval process can take
I'll also share the timeline of an earlier trademark application, from filing in May through examination, publication, and the opposition period.

media:group.media:description:
ENSv2 is moving toward activation, and the DAO vote is now live. If you own a .eth name, what does this mean for renewal prices, migration, and your existing names?
I used AI to investigate the ENSv2 proposal and verify the official sources. Then I built an AI presenter to explain the changes.
In this video, we cover the proposed increase from $5 to $8 per year for 5+ character names, multi-year renewal discounts, the shorter grace period, voluntary migration, and what owners should know before making an irreversible move.

entry.title: I Gave an AI Agent an SEO Job. Now It Works Without Me.

media:group.media:title: I Gave an AI Agent an SEO Job. Now It Works Without Me.
media:group.media:description:
I built an AI agent that finds five new websites every day, creates accounts, verifies emails, and links back to my personal website. The best part? It does the work without me.
In this video, I show you how I built this fully autonomous workflow using HyperAgent, starting with a simple conversation.
The goal was straightforward: find legitimate, free websites where I could create professional profiles and build my online presence. I didn't want to spend hours researching sites, filling out forms, uploading headshots, or verifying email addresses.
So I gave the entire job to an AI agent.
It researches opportunities, evaluates websites, creates accounts where possible, handles email verification through its own Gmail account, and tracks everything. If it can't complete a signup independently, it skips that site and moves on.
I walk through the actual system, including:
- How I got started with HyperAgent and why I still use it - The difference between an AI chat and an AI agent - How to choose between different AI models - The original conversation that started the project - The working notes, biographies, headshots, and other information the agent assembled - Why I give AI agents dedicated email accounts - The tracker, completed profiles, and daily automation - How similar workflows could be built with other agent platforms, including Hermes and GrokBot
I've been experimenting with HyperAgent for about six months. I originally tried it after receiving $10,000 in promotional credits from attending a session at NYC Tech Week. This video is not sponsored. I'm sharing my experience with a tool I've genuinely enjoyed using.
One important distinction: creating backlinks doesn't guarantee improved search rankings. I'm focusing on legitimate, relevant profiles rather than spam directories, and I'll need to measure whether this experiment produces meaningful SEO results.
What interests me most isn't SEO. It's what happens when we give AI agents real responsibilities and let them work independently.
I'm building things, testing new technology, and sharing what actually happens, including the successes, failures, and surprises.
**What repetitive task would you give an AI agent?** I'd love to hear what you're experimenting with.
